# homelab-zerofs

ZeroFS as a CSI driver: a leader/standby gateway pair holds one POSIX filesystem inside an S3
bucket, and `csi.zerofs.net` hands out directories of that filesystem as PersistentVolumes mounted
over 9P. **Installed by cluster-admin** into `zerofs`.

## Why its own chart

Foundational, same rationale as `topolvm`/`cilium`: a cluster-scoped CSI driver whose node plugin is
privileged, opens `/dev/fuse`, and mounts into the kubelet's tree. The autonomous operator can't
install that, so it lives outside the `app-*`/`tool-*` namespaces Kyverno governs.

## Why a second CSI driver

`topolvm-provisioner` carves logical volumes out of a node's own NVMe: fast, and unreachable from
any other node. A workload that needs `ReadWriteMany`, or that must survive the loss of the node its
data landed on, has nowhere to put its data today. ZeroFS volumes are directories on a filesystem
that lives in object storage, so any number of pods on any number of nodes mount the same one, and a
rescheduled pod finds its data from wherever it lands.

The two are complements, not alternatives. Everything latency-bound — databases, etcd, the
SeaweedFS volumes themselves — belongs on TopoLVM. ZeroFS is for shared and durable state, and its
read path is a local cache in front of a remote object store.

## The gateway pair

ZeroFS is single-writer per storage path, so the driver shares one gateway across every volume of
its StorageClass rather than starting a process per volume. Availability comes from a standby: the
leader ships writes before acknowledging them, and on heartbeat silence the standby claims a durable
marker, epoch-fences the old writer through the object store, and takes over. Published mounts block
through the gap and resume by inode id — a failover is not a remount. This is failover, not
write scale-out; two nodes, one writer, always.

Both halves are configured identically apart from their identity and their bootstrap role hint, and
both must name the same storage URL and encryption password — they are two views of one filesystem,
not two filesystems. The `role` in the config is only a hint: at startup each node asks its peer who
is leading, so a restarted node does not fence a live leader.

Readiness deliberately probes the replication port rather than 9P. A standby binds replication early
to receive ships and answer heartbeats, but binds 9P only once it takes over; probing 9P would drop
the standby from its Service and cut off the stream it exists to consume.

## Trust boundary

None of the gateway's ports authenticates anything, exactly like NFS with `AUTH_SYS`: 9P's attach
name is namespacing, not authorization, and the admin RPC runs every call as uid 0 with the power to
delete any volume. Reachability is therefore the entire security model, and the chart's
CiliumNetworkPolicy is load-bearing rather than defence in depth — it is what stops any pod in the
cluster from attaching to the filesystem root. Data is encrypted before it reaches the object store,
with a key wrapped by the encryption password, so the bucket's own credentials do not read it.

## Credentials

The chart creates no credential Secret and takes no literal key, so nothing sensitive reaches a
values file or the release history. Create the Secret named by `gateway.secretName` in the `zerofs`
namespace first, holding `encryptionPassword`, `accessKeyId` and `secretAccessKey`; the rendered
config references them as `${VAR}` and ZeroFS expands them at start.

The encryption password wraps the storage key rather than being it, so it can be rotated with
`zerofs change-password` without rewriting data — but losing it loses the filesystem. Changing it in
the Secret without running that command leaves the pair unable to open the store.

## Storage backend

`gateway.storage.url` has no default and the install fails without one. ZeroFS fences writers with
put-if-not-exists, so the backend must fail a conditional PUT against an existing object instead of
overwriting it; a store that answers success needs `conditional_put` pointed at a Redis, or both
halves of the pair can come to believe they lead. Verify that before pointing this at an S3
implementation rather than assuming it.

Whatever tier is chosen must be hot and instant-access. ZeroFS reads the manifest, the SSTs and
segment objects continuously, so an archive class makes the filesystem unreadable rather than
merely slow, and an infrequent-access class usually costs more than the hot one.

## Install

```sh
kubectl create namespace zerofs
kubectl -n zerofs create secret generic zerofs \
  --from-literal=encryptionPassword=... \
  --from-literal=accessKeyId=... \
  --from-literal=secretAccessKey=...
helm install zerofs zerofs -n zerofs
```

Nodes need `/dev/fuse`; the node plugin mounts it from the host and fails to publish without it.

## Limits worth knowing before adopting it

- **PVC sizes are labels.** Capacity is not enforced per volume; the gateway's filesystem quota is
  the only ceiling, and it covers every volume at once.
- **Restarting the node plugin breaks that node's mounts.** The FUSE clients are its children, so
  the DaemonSet updates `OnDelete` and an upgrade is a per-node, drain-first operation.
- **No per-volume snapshots.** ZeroFS checkpoints cover the whole filesystem.
- **Mount volumes only.** `volumeMode: Block` is unsupported; a workload needing a fixed-size disk
  can create an image file inside its volume.
- **StorageClass `mountOptions` are rejected**, not ignored.
